speechtext:
Hon. members will be glad to know, I am sure, that I shall not unduly delay consideration of this measure by the House. However, I feel it is incumbent upon me at least to outline in the House the position I have already taken outside the House and in my riding in particular. It is not a new position for me by any means. I have had experience of so-called independent electoral boundary commissions in jurisdictions other than this. The fact that I now represent a rural riding has not changed my opinion with respect to previously held convictions which I expressed when I represented a congested urban riding in another jurisdiction. The theory of an independent Electoral Boundaries Commission, presumably free from gross, partisan political considerations, is excellent but in practice it leaves much to be desired.
I complained bitterly when in another jurisdiction I was confronted with legislation almost similar to the bill we are considering in the federal field. I do not understand how those in the federal jurisdiction can commit the same blunders that people in other jurisdictions have made. In some cases the federal people have picked the same personnel for the boundary commissions that the provincial people have picked, despite the errors of the past. Here, as usual, the federal jurisdiction drags along, like a cow's tail, behind provincial jurisdictions in legislation that has been enacted at the provincial level, even when everyone at the provincial level is willing to admit that the province made a mistake. As I said, the theory is good, but it does not work in practice. The history of electoral boundary commissions at both provincial and federal levels proves this.
Somehow or other these commissions are imbued with the ideas of the engineering concepts, with the concept that takes into account only population figures. That is why I welcome the government's move in this respect to hoist for 18 months the whole operation of the Electoral Boundaries Commission. When I say that, I wish that some of these considerations had been taken into account earlier by the government so that we would not be in our present position, because many people, including editorial writers, are taking jabs at us for undoing what they believe to be progressive legislation. It is not progressive legislation in that it simply does not work.
In deciding electoral boundaries one should not only look at bare population figures; one should also look at communities of interest, at municipal boundaries and at municipal electoral and provincial electoral boundaries. The people of this country find most confusing the fact that municipal boundaries are different from provincial electoral boundaries, which in turn are different from federal electoral boundaries. Surely, in these days when mankind can put men on the moon, it should not be difficult for political administrations in this country to get together and work out a realistic and workable system under which municipal electoral boundaries, provincial
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension electoral boundaries and federal electoral boundaries can more closely coincide with one another than they do today.
In the province of Ontario, particularly southern Ontario, there is a hodge-podge of electoral districts, It is my hope that in the 18 months or so that lie ahead of us when this matter will be considered and, hopefully, a more permanent solution will be found, we shall come up with an answer which will make possible some sort of working agreement with provincial and municipal authorities. I hope that a more permanent body will be set up to look into the question of boundaries affecting all three levels of government. Hopefully, it will do so more realistically than these so-called independent commissions.
There is another matter I shall mention, although I feel that I should not talk about it. It is this. The general area of southern Ontario, part of which I represent at the moment, returns 11 members to this House. Of those-I am speaking strictly from memory-eight are Progressive Conservatives, two are Liberals, of whom one is a cabinet minister, and one is a member of the NDP. In the first report of the Ontario Electoral Boundaries Commission, made earlier, changes were made in almost all those 11 seats. Some of the members concerned objected, some political organizations objected and some citizens' groups objected. Some of us did not object because we were aware of the problems that exist in satisfying the great conflicts that obviously appear when something like this is attempted. In any event, opportunity was given to the public and to politicians to object to that first report. Many people took advantage of that opportunity.
Sir, this bill having been given first reading, I found it rather odd, to put it mildly, that the next day the second report of the Ontario Electoral Boundaries Commission came out. No more public hearings could be held in connection with that report or, rather, there could be no more hearings unless there was filed a notice of dispute or a notice of objection. I would have thought that the Ontario commission would have realized that the first reading of this bill indicated that the government intended to bring about drastic changes in this area or at least to put things on ice, as it were, for 18 months. Instead, the Ontario commissioners presented their second report the day after this bill had been read the first time. That report was released to the press and tabled in this House. I find that strange. I do not know why that could not have been held until the House had finished its deliberations in respect of the measure now before us. That is my first point.
My second point is this. I am rather suspicious, being of a cynical turn of mind, of the drastic alterations proposed for many ridings of southeastern Ontario. Of those 11 seats, eight are held by Conservatives, two by Liberals and one by the NDP. I find it passing strange that only the Tory seats were to be affected. The two Liberal seats were really not affected at all, and the one NDP seat was not affected. I am afraid that in my senile dotage I am getting rather suspicious and cynical about some of these things. In any event, the people I represent were rather upset about the second report as they did not have any oportuni-ty to make representations to the commission about it. I think the legislation is therefore deficient, because the tabling of that second report means that unless notice of

July 19, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension dispute is filed within 30 days after its tabling in the House, those boundaries become law, or would become law except for the provisions of the measure that we are now debating. There is no opportunity for public hearings to be held.
My point to you today, Sir, is that that second or final report of the Ontario Electoral Boundaries Commission so drastically changes the first report as really to make the two reports completely irreconcilable. Therefore I think, even though it is a brand new report and one which has not seen the light of day before the people in my riding particularly, or in the neighbouring riding where the people are equally upset about it, there will be no opportunity for these people to make public their grievances or complain about it at a public hearing.
That is why I shall vote for the government measure that is before us today. I think this is rather unreal legislation, and therefore I believe an 18 month hoist is good. I also do not intend to support the amendment of my good and valued colleague the hon. member for Peel South simply because I think that a 12 month period is not long enough. A period of at least 18 months will be required to try to straighten out the mess we are now in.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assure you and the members of the House that I shall not speak long in this debate. I believe, however, that there are a couple of factors which should be mentioned. The committee which will be set up will have the obligation in some way or other of bringing about equity between the provinces. In the province of Alberta the Electoral Boundaries Commission paid definite attention to the proposed growth factor and little attention to the 25 per cent variance factor. We have had city ridings with smaller populations than so-called rural ridings in which there has been a variance, in some cases, of 16,000, yet in the new redistribution in the province of Ontario, for example, this is not the case. Some of the rural ridings could go down as low as
54,000	in the new redistribution and some could go as high as 98,000. But nowhere do we see this same balance hold true in respect of Alberta or Manitoba. I have not looked at the situation in the province of New Brunswick but I am told that there too the preference is given to the growth centres and not the sparsely populated areas.
The other factor which I think the committee should study and which also will take some time-and therefore I am not really inclined to support the amendment of the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn)-is the floor for provinces which may well have a slower rate of growth than the general average for Canada. I am thinking here particularly of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The present floor in the British North America Act, as we all know, in essence is the same number of Commons seats as the province has Senate seats. This gives a province like Prince Edward Island, with little more than 100,000 people, four seats in the House of Commons because it has four seats in the Senate. It gives New Brunswick and Nova Scotia a floor of ten seats while the province of Saskatchewan, which has a population similar to that of Nova Scotia, could well go down to the point where it has a floor of six seats.

In this day and age when all eyes are focused on the west and the new feeling of alienation which may have come to light here in Ottawa I think it behooves the members of this legislature to attempt to justify this inequity which appears in the redistribution act. Certainly we should give this matter a lot of thought. I do think that in doing that we should necessarily enlarge the membership of the House of Commons. From the attendance which has been evident in some committees it is possible that an enlarged House of Commons would allow for greater participation by members in committees, which would therefore allow more committees to function. But I really do not think that has been the real problem in respect of committees. I know that the larger the House of Commons becomes in membership perhaps the more unwieldly it becomes; also the more democratic the process becomes the more voices we hear from the people. However, I think the House could become pretty unwieldy.
I would not be opposed to a minor alteration in the membership of the House of Commons. When I was first elected the membership was 265. Our population has grown. It is hard to equate how the responsibilities of a member of parliament grow, but they have grown. The government seems to be rushing forward in its attempt to do things for people. In this attempt to do things for people we are seeing more and more government participation in business all across Canada. This causes a great deal of concern to many people. That concern, of course, is registered with their representative in the House of Commons. So while we might expect a minor increase in the House of Commons, I do not think it is necessary to consider a figure of 299 or something like that. I do not think we need go that far.
I think a formula in respect of a base for Manitoba and Saskatchewan can be arrived at with less enlargement than that of the House of Commons. Certainly with the spirit of conciliation which has taken place in Ottawa I think this committee of the House of Commons, when formed, would like to hear briefs from the provinces, particularly Saskatchewan and Manitoba, concerning the question of a floor for representation in the House of Commons. This could take some time. I have participated extensively in committee work and I know how difficult it sometimes is to get committees to arrive at a point where what might be called a consensus of opinion is reached in respect of the issuance of a report back to the House. Sometimes this takes a long time.
I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the House which reminds me of an occasion when it took a period of about a year and a half to reach a consensus on a bill in the committee on agriculture. I do not suppose this committee would take quite that long, but I do know that we require the length of time the bill suggests. I believe we would be running an undue risk if we were to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Peel South in his amendment to shorten the time period from 18 months to 12 months.
This is a problem which has plagued Canada. If redistribution must take place after each census-and I am not opposed to that-then we must make certain that it takes place in a fair and equitable manner in respect of all
July 19, 1973

regions of Canada and all segments of society. A little extra time would be well spent in settling some of the grievances which have been voiced in this and other debates in the House of Commons.
The question of adequate representation of rural and urban areas is another problem. I do think that as legislators we should be attacking that problem; we should be attempting to solve it. Because of the differences in the findings of the electoral commissions in the various provinces, I do not think they can solve that problem. In fact, they have aggravated it to some degree. Also, no attempt has been made to solve the matter of the floor which I have mentioned.
For that reason I think that the House should not accept the amendment, although I realize the concern of the hon. member for Peel South regarding the huge size of his constituency and I certainly understand the motivation behind his amendment. However, I want to say to him through you, Mr. Speaker, that knowing the energy which he possesses I am sure that he is quite capable of representing that huge riding for the additional six months or so, no matter how long it takes to arrive at an equitable solution. I think that the people in Peel South are well represented and with his energy the hon. member will be able to do a good job in the additional six months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened intently to the discussions that have taken place on this bill and I was particularly interested, as we all should be, in the remarks that were made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen). We have considered the problem of redistribution on several occasions
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
and therefore I am concerned about the government's intentions. I am sure that the people in northern Ontario would like better representation and this may be brought about by the time the government gets around to doing something about it.
Just last week a new agency has been established in northern Ontario whose purpose is to establish a new province in that area. I wish them well, and I certainly hope they will have some success. We have the problem of urban versus rural representation, the problem of distances and of floors, in fact all of the various problems that we were faced with in 1964. These problems have not gone away and some of them have been partly solved.
I have been very concerned about some of my colleagues in northern Ontario. One in particular did not have any interest in this matter and did not even bother making a representation to the judge, as did many other people. He ended up in a very bad situation, and it serves him right; he damn well deserves it. Anything that he got was of his own making. However, that does not change the situation for other members. I would be quite happy to go along with the boundaries which we now have, not so much because I am satisfied but because it would put him in such a bad position that it would please me to see him struggle a bit.
The point I would like to make on third reading is that I wish the House leader could outline what he wants and how long he thinks the review will take. He has said that it will take 18 months, but I do not think it can be done in 18 months unless we start right now. I am sure that we will not get started on this for a long period of time. If we are to do something about it, it seems to me that the President of the Privy Council will have to say that he is prepared to establish a committee immediately to assess what we can do about this matter.
Much has been said about the redistribution which we accepted in 1965. I think that the 25 per cent tolerance for each province is a pretty good system. I think we have a problem in some areas, and northern Ontario is one of them. I sympathize with the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), who represents a very large area which may be enlarged in such a way that it will be very difficult to service. The same has been true for me for a long time.
The boundaries of the riding of Timmins are a disgrace, but from another point of view. No distances were involved. It was easy to represent. Sudbury is another riding of which the same can be said. In northern Ontario we are really not competing with Toronto for urban representation, but Sudbury was the kind of riding that was easy to represent.
I think that the re-distribution was fairly reasonable and in accordance with the terms that we gave to the commission. I know that in my own instance the commissioners looked at northern Ontario and recognized that it was a big area and that they would be foolish to travel across it. There are really no good maps of northern Ontario except for lakes and forests, and no one would try to divide an area which covers three quarters of Ontario. But they did take into consideration the information they were given by us and they did make a number of changes. They gave the public an opportunity to make representations. I was not in complete agreement with the represen-
5804

July 19, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension tation that was made to the commission in Kirkland Lake and in Timiskaming, but the people made their representations to the commission and the commissioners listened to them and accepted pretty well their proposals. They redrew northern Ontario on the basis of those representations. I think that the commissioners did listen and did give the public the opportunity to speak out.
I do not think it really matters how long the review will take, whether it is three months, 12 months or 18 months. It depends on what we intend to do in that time. The House leader can ask for 18 months. I presume that he is thinking what most of us are thinking, namely that it will not affect us because there will be an election before that time. If nothing happens in that time and we come back, perhaps we will reinstate the boundaries commissions and start all over again. I do not think that is good enough. I think we have met the needs of members of parliament but we have not done much for the country. What the President of the Privy Council should do is to set down a timetable.
I listened with great interest to the speech of the President of the Privy Council. He knows the reasons why the job cannot be done within much less than 18 months, but he said nothing about establishing a committee to do the job. Surely we will not get back to the position where the government party can gerrymander.
A few minutes ago I heard another opposition member say he was looking with a jaundiced eye on what the commission had done in his area because greater displacement in opposition seats took place than in government seats. Or perhaps he meant that the NDP seat in that area had not been changed. Who he was accusing, I do not know. But I hold that if the government House leader is serious he should be prepared to give an indication on third reading of what he is going to do about the problem.
The period of 18 months may not be too long, but it will not give us too much time if he lets 12 months go by before starting to act. Here we are sitting in Ottawa in the month of July when we should be on holiday, and we may sit on into August. The government House leader knows that what he is doing may make it impossible for us to have a summer holiday next year also. I was one of a number of people who worked to establish a regular, organized summer holiday in June, July and August, but we loused it up by not having a real timetable and by not being prepared to make decisions early.
If we are serious about having an election under a new system of redistribution, we should set down a timetable for that redistribution. Will we have a special committee undertake the job? Will we bring in officials from the redistribution commission as well? Will we establish an impartial committee to which members of parliament will have some input? When will the job start?
If the government House leader is not prepared to get up on third reading and give us a timetable, nothing may happen until next spring. In that case we could have ar election on the basis of the old boundaries and we might not have to worry about this problem for another four years, although I suspect we would have to start worrying about it two months after the next election since I do not

think the result of that election would be much different from the last.
A constitutional amendment may also be necessary. In that case there are two sides to the issue. We may have to ask the provinces to give up their Senate floor, or we may add new Senate floor bases for a number of provinces that have been losing population. In that event we would need an amendment to the BNA Act, and this would require the co-operation of the provinces. With one exception we have not been able to amend the BNA Act since 1913 without the unanimous consent of the parties involved.
I think this discussion has been worthwhile although general in nature. Within limits I have always taken the word of the President of the Privy Council as gospel, and I am willing to accept what he says in outlining a timetable to bring together the diverse elements not only in the House of Commons but throughout the country when dealing with redistribution.
I believe we should benefit from the work already done by the boundary commissions. We would be stupid if we did not give some consideration to their deliberations. If the President of the Privy Council does not make a statement on third reading, then I hope he will discuss this matter with his cabinet colleagues and be prepared to give us a timetable in the very near future. I think the 18 month period should date from now, not from five or six months hence.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: WHEAT-HIGHER PRICE TO MILLERS TO REFLECT CURRENT WORLD PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Governor in Council has approved a change instructing the Canadian Wheat Board to charge Canadian millers a higher price for wheat reflecting current world price.
In order to avoid the total of the increase going on the price of bread, the government will pay $1 per bushel as a continuation of its two-price wheat policy. The balance, and never less than $2, will be paid to the Canadian Wheat Board by domestic millers, basis 1 Canadian Wheat Red Spring Wheat at Thunder Bay.
Under the previous two-price wheat scheme, in effect since 1971, the Wheat Board charged domestic millers $1,951/2 per bushel and the government paid $1,041/2. This guaranteed farmers a $3 return for milling wheat used in Canada. The important thing to western farmers is that wheat sold to domestic millers will reflect the world price, and farmers will always be assured of no less than $3 per bushel.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: Always?

subtopic: WHEAT-HIGHER PRICE TO MILLERS TO REFLECT CURRENT WORLD PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take the opportunity to thank the minister for sending a copy of the proposed statement to my office. We appreciate that very much, particularly in view of the statement's brevity and its poor explanation of what the minister is really doing. If I misinterpret the statement in any way I ask the forgiveness of the House and the minister; it is because of his rather poor explanation.
The way I interpret this statement, it limits the liability of the government. Up until this time, if the world price of wheat continued to rise and it reached, say, $4 a bushel, in
Wheat Price Increase
ordering the Wheat Board to sell to millers at $1.95Vi, the government's liability would reach close to or above the $2 mark.
One must always acknowledge the fact that the executive must be better informed than the opposition, must be better informed than backbenchers in any party because they have a huge staff researching world conditions. I have had some arguments with the minister about what world prices of wheat do, but it is obvious from this statement that the minister is frightened about the obligation the government might have to assume if his expectations are correct that world wheat prices will continue to rise. The statement says quite clearly:
In order to avoid the total of the increase going on the price of bread, the government will pay $1 per bushel as a continuation of its two-price wheat policy.
The key word there is "total"-in order to avoid the total of the increase going on the price of bread. He is not necessarily saying there will be no increase in the price of bread; he is saying that part of the increase will be borne by the government.
There has been some mention in this place in recent days of the high price of food. Here is a government contribution to what the low price of bread is going to be.
The second last paragraph states that to date the government has paid $1,041/2 per bushel. They are going to lower their contribution. They expect the price of wheat to go higher, so we can expect the price of bread in Canada to go up in the near future. The government is somewhat frightened by the trend in world prices and about their liability, so they come forward with this concept now in order to make it abundantly clear that they will only be liable for another dollar a bushel and that is all.
It behooves one at this time to look at world prices. Depending on what port you buy from in Canada, whether Vancouver, Thunder Bay or Churchill, I think it is safe to say they are hovering in the neighbourhood of $3.50 per bushel. So the increase in the price of wheat to the miller is in the neighbourhood of 35 cents to 40 cents a bushel.
It is interesting to note that in his statement the minister says the balance paid to the Canadian Wheat Board by domestic millers shall never be less than $2. Even in the statement the minister is acknowledging the increase to the miller from $1,951/2 to at least $2. It will never be less than $2.

I am disappointed that the House does not wish me to explain my position, as one who represents people living in urban areas. It seems the urban parts of Canada sometimes get pushed around here.
I am also disappointed that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) should have suggested to Your Honour that you ought to intervene. I was about to indicate to the House that those who live in urban Canada do appreciate the position of people who come from rural areas. It is clear to me from the speech made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) that the whole question of redistribution is now being thrust back into a cocked hat. The efforts which have been made year after year, census after census, to deal with the growth in population and with changes in the distribution of population, culminating in the act passed in 1964, are to be thrown out of the window.
A number of difficult issues have been presented to the House. The first is the question of amendments to the British North America Act involving the minimum representation that each province should receive. I made a suggestion earlier as to the manner in which this might be approached. Then there was the question whether the independent commissions have done their work properly in accordance with section 13(b) of the act. Did they really pay attention to 13(b) in some parts of Canada? This should be a relatively easy matter for the House to determine. The President of the Privy Council suggests that the bill before us, by imposing a hiatus, will resolve this difficulty. I am not sure it will, but at least it is an attempt to do so.
We have heard the suggestion made a number of times during the debate that members of parliament do not represent people at all but represent areas of land. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, what I said during the debate on second reading. I do not represent areas of land, or apartment buildings, or airport runways, any more than the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) represents areas in the province of Ontario called townships. He represents people and I represent people.
The people of urban Canada are prepared to say that the size of some urban constituencies does give rise to difficulty, and that the use of the permitted 25 per cent variation is the way to deal with this situation. That is what the act says, and this is what should be done. But apparently in certain areas some people are not satisfied with this provision. They say that because their community has always been represented by a member of parliament in the past, it should always be so represented in the future and that is all there is to it. Even if their community does not grow as the rest of Canada has grown, or fails to grow in the same proportion, they feel they are still entitled to the same representation.
This amounts to saying that the size of the House should be increased by a large number of members every decennial census. Because as I have already pointed out in this debate, the population of Canada has doubled since 1940. On this basis, if we had started back in 1940 with 245
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension members, the House would now consist of 590 members. So an approach of this kind is not a solution.
All of us, as members of the House, like the status quo. Usually we all like the comfortable pew. We do not really desire change that much. But change is taking place in our society. There is movement of people away from the country. Or, rather, the increase in our population is in the urban areas. And it is a huge increase. We shall not find a way out of this dilemma by ignoring all the effort and energy expended over the years since confederation in working out a reasonably fair, independent-commission-oriented redistribution act just because some people in this chamber say they may have to do more work, that they may have to represent more people. That is the way it is. Canada is growing. Members of parliament will have to represent more people and they will have to work harder. One of the reasons redistribution is necessary is to spread the load more evenly.
Trees do not write letters. Rivers do not write letters. Shorelines do not write letters. Roads do not write letters. It is people who write letters. It is people who wish to make their views known. To suggest that people in certain parts of Canada have less to complain about because they are crowded together in highrise apartments is utter nonsense. I can understand the inconvenience encountered by members whose ridings are being increased in size. Of course there will be an increase in their workload. And to the extent that my constituency, along with others, would be reduced in size, the workload would be reduced. But this is the way Canada is going.
Canada is becoming a great nation. The way to reduce the impact of a heavier workload is surely not simply to add more members to this chamber. No, Mr. Speaker; the solution lies in giving existing members the machinery and technical assistance which they will increasingly need. The leader of the Social Credit Party, for example, represents a huge rural riding. Is there anything wrong about supplying him with free airplane service around that constituency so that he can see his people? Isn't that what we should be doing? Is there anything wrong about seeing he gets the best facilities possible for telephone communication with his constituents? Perhaps this is the way we should be handling such a situation. He tells us his riding extends for 600 miles in one direction and an awfully long way in the other, and that it takes him 15 days to get round it. We must make it possible for him to get round that riding. This can easily be done in this modern age of fast transportation.
In throwing out the existing act-and we are throwing it out with the bath water-we are saying that our efforts in the 60's, in the Pearson years, to organize redistribution on a non-partisan basis, to get rid of the old gerrymandering, were wasted. Apparently we are prepared to go back to what we had before, to political influence, to what is called political input today. It used to be called gerrymandering; today it is political input.
These troubles have plagued us since confederation. One can read the kind of speeches which have been made in this debate in Hansard of previous years. The speeches were made up to the time of the passing of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING CERTAIN IMMIGRATION LAWS AND PROCEDURES
speechtext:
that Bill C-212, respecting certain immigration laws and procedures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to start by assuring hon. members of this House, who may be rather surprised to see me back so soon again with another bill dealing with immigration, that I am not trying to presume on the goodwill and the all-party co-operation that existed when Bill C-197 was before the House a few days ago. I have to be honest and tell them I am somewhat surprised to be here in this situation, but two recent and unexpected events threaten to weaken substantially the very foundation of progress in immigration matters after the all-party support of Bill C-197 and really would have the effect of sending us back to square one.
As hon. members will no doubt recall, the change in the immigration regulations of last fall, which revoked section 34 of those regulations, was intended at that time to prevent would-be immigrants pouring into the country in the guise of visitors, with the intention of seeking landed immigrant status once they got here on the strength of regulation 34. In recalling this, hon. members will also remember that one of the goals of Bill C-197 was to ensure that from now on refused applicants for landed immigrant status would not be able to stay on in Canada with impunity or be subject to delay in getting a decision about their appeal.
Immigration
During the debate and study at all stages of Bill C-197, I certainly sensed a general agreement in this House that Canada must have the right to screen future residents of this country before they establish residence here, and indeed that those who fail to pass that screening should not be able to stay here in defiance of Canadian immigration policy.
The two events to which I have referred which threaten to undermine the efforts of parliament to restore order to the immigration process are two recent decisions interpreting immigration law, one by the Immigration Appeal Board within the last two weeks or so, and one by the Federal Court of Appeal just prior to that.
In the process of discussing these decisions and their implications I want to emphasize I in no way wish to criticize the Immigration Appeal Board or the Federal Court of Appeal for either decision, although I do in fact disagree with them. Both those judicial bodies have the responsibility to interpret the law as written and as they see it. Certainly in meeting that responsibility quite clearly it is the text of the law which they must interpret and not necessarily the intent of the government in drafting that law.
The problem we now face is that either of these decisions alone could have a very serious impact on the administration of immigration law. When put together, just as we are about to put a new immigration policy into effect, the result is that their combined effect would be that the administrative system would be hopelessly overburdened and that in fact the props would be knocked from under all our efforts to restore order to the immigration process.
The result of the Immigration Appeal Board decision, to put it in the most simple and practical terms possible, is to restore the effect of regulation 34 which before its revocation enabled visitors to apply and qualify within Canada for landed immigrant status. When this regulation 34 was revoked last November or last fall, the companion regulation dealing with visa requirements, regulation 28(1), was also amended to require that immigrants, whether seeking admission at a port of entry or applying for landed immigrant status after entry in another category, must in fact have an immigrant visa. As hon. members know, immigrant visas are issued only at posts outside Canada. Short of amending the Immigration Act itself at that time, this was the only means at our disposal for heading off a continued flow of applications by visitors landing in Canada in spite of the revocation of regulation 34. Lacking a visa, applicants in Canada could, as a result of this amendment to regulation 28(1), be reported for special inquiry which could lead to an order for deportation.
The Immigration Appeal Board has now ruled in its recent decision that the amendment of the regulation dealing with immigrant visa requirements went beyond the power that the Immigration Act gives the governor in council to make regulations. In legal terms this decision, if upheld, could mean that applicants in Canada would not be required to have immigrant visas, which also means that the last legal hold on them would be thus lost. In practical terms, as I have mentioned, it would mean that the effect of regulation 34 would be restored-in fact the situation would be worse than when regulation 34 was

July 19, 1973
Immigration
valid-and that some 1,750 appeals against deportation orders may be upheld because the orders were made on grounds that the board has now had occasion to find to be legally invalid.
The second decision, that of the Federal Court of Appeal, deals with applications made under regulation 34 before it was revoked. Putting that decision in simple terms, it says that my department has had no jurisdiction over these many years to make deportation orders against persons who applied for landing in Canada and who after examination were in fact refused. In this case some 10,000 appeals against such deportation orders before the Immigration Appeal Board are affected.
In light of this federal court decision, all of these applications could be allowed. We have always taken the position, in the belief that it was fully supported by the law, that a person who applied in Canada for landing under regulation 34 ceased in fact, in legal terms, to be a non-immigrant and was reporting for examination as required by subsection 7(3) of the Immigration Act. That position has been backed up for many years by judicial decisions. The recent federal court decision that is now giving us trouble reverses those prior judgments.
The key subsection 7(3) of the Immigration Act reads:
Where any person who entered Canada as a non-immigrant ceases to be a non-immigrant or to be in the particular class in which he was admitted as a non-immigrant and, in either case, remains in Canada, he shall forthwith report such facts to the nearest immigration officer and present himself for examination at such time and place as he may be directed and shall, for the purposes of the examination and all other purposes under this act, be deemed to be a person seeking admission to Canada.
This subsection, together with succeeding sections of the act, gave authority, which we still hold to be valid, for an applicant's examination as an immigrant, in the legal sense of the word, defined in the act as "a person who seeks admission to Canada for permanent residence". It was from this that the authority came, if the applicant failed to meet the requirements for landed immigrant status, for his or her referral to a special inquiry officer and for the making of a deportation order if the special inquiry officer found that this was warranted.
However, the Federal Court of Appeal has now ruled that a person who applied under regulation 34 while it was in effect until November of last year did not lose his non-immigrant status. According to this ruling, again if it were upheld, the application was not the report referred to in subsection 7(3), as we had believed, and consequently there was no authority for the special inquiry or deportation order.
I do not think it is necessary for me to draw a picture for hon. members of what the consequences of this would do to Canada's image of a country able to control the admission of immigrants to this country, or to the horrendous workload which these two decisions could impose on the administration of our immigration system, coming at a time when the House would not, under ordinary circumstances, be in session, at a time when we have just introduced the adjustment of status program, with the special workload that that will entail, and also at a time when the tourist season is at its absolute peak.

Under both decisions we would be faced with a huge backlog of cases to reassess in light of an uncertain legal position. Under one decision we would be faced with another inundation of false visitors, such as we experienced last year. I would remind hon. members that we reached the peak one October weekend last fall when some 4,500 people arrived by plane at Malton, ostensibly as visitors but mostly with the intention of staying in Canada. This inundation of visitors that we experienced last year will most likely be repeated as these decisions become known around the world, and that will be very quickly, as I find is the case as I get experience in this portfolio.
This whole thing adds up to the fact that the new provisions of Bill C-197 will never get off the ground. I have some consideration for the disappointments that would arise as a result of the false hopes and expectations of people abroad, often very innocent people, who would act upon this and come to Canada, when it really is this Parliament's intention not to repeat the experience that we tried to correct the other day in Bill C-197. I would also draw to the attention of hon. members the danger of the exploitation of many innocent people by unscrupulous so-called immigration counsellors, who could take the substance of these decisions and convince innocent people to come to Canada, many of whom in countries we can all name and who would do anything to come to this country to get away from the circumstances in which they are presently living.
That is not a happy picture. As I emphasized earlier, I mean no criticism of the Immigration Appeal Board or the Federal Court of Appeal. As the minister responsible, I am seeking leave to appeal both decisions and I would be quite prepared to take my chances on the outcome of those appeals, assuming leave to appeal is granted. But I do not think we can collectively, as parliamentarians, afford to risk the possibility, under the circumstances that I have described of this House not being in session and of it hitting us when the peak load of genuine visitors are coming to the country, that leave may not be granted. Nor do I think we can risk the possibility of having to wait out a period of several months at least during which time these appeals are being considered.
I am acutely aware of the fact that, having just emphasized to hon. members the urgency of Bill C-197, I am again making a similar plea in favour of quick action for this legislation. I know that I could soon begin to sound, if I kept this up, as if I were crying "wolf". But I do think that the room that has been made in the timetable of this House, under these circumstances and at this stage of the session, speaks eloquently for the government's view of the emergency that faces us.
Bill C-212, to put it briefly and in layman's terms, seeks the sanction of Parliament for the regulation stipulating that all immigrants, in the sense of the word as defined in the Immigration Act, must have immigrant visas, no matter where they undergo examination. It would give the sanction of Parliament to the long established understanding that people who applied for landing under former regulation 34 did indeed cease to be non-immigrant and became immigrants, thus subject to examination and, as necessary, inquiry and a deportation order. Perhaps most
July 19, 1973

important, it would apply to all cases already dealt with by administrators but not yet finally concluded on appeal.
There are two important observations I would like to make at this point. First, I have always felt, and I am sure many hon. members would agree with me, that legislation that is in any real sense retroactive, unless of course it confers retroactive benefits, which nobody objects to, is repugnant. By retroactive legislation in that sense I mean basically a retroactive change in the rules of the game.
I must recognize that this bill, in an extremely legalistic sense, could be regarded as retroactive because it applies to persons who had been reported for special inquiry, or ordered deported, before it was introduced. But really, Mr. Speaker, I think those who examine the bill and sense the intent will realize that, rather than seeking to change the rules, it seeks to maintain the rules as they have been operating for many years-in the case of regulation 34 from its introduction six years ago in 1967 to its revocation in 1972.
The fact is that the rules for which this bill now seeks the ultimate sanction of Parliament, under the circumstances of emergency that I have described, are the rules that have been known and have been applied to all who have come to this country as non-immigrants and who have later sought permanent residence. The bill takes from no one any right that she or he had once enjoyed or had any real reason to expect to enjoy.
I also want to emphasize, re-emphasize and underline that nothing in this bill will affect the adjustment of status program that was included in Bill C-197. I really cannot stress too much or repeat too often that people should have no fear that their eligibility to register for that program, which is about to be launched and which had universal support in this House, will in any way be impaired by the provisions of Bill C-212. This legislation simply does not apply to people eligible for that program, and it will go forward as planned.
Before I conclude my opening remarks in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I do want to call attention to the fact that a minor typographical error was made in printing, of which I will seek correction in committee.
I think I could sum it up by saying that Bill C-212, through force of circumstances-recent decisions of the court-has become a necessary companion piece to Bill C-197. Without it, Bill C-197 might well fail to achieve the objectives we all agreed upon we wanted to seek. With this bill, if it meets the approval of hon. members, conversely Bill C-197 is virtually assured of success. In that light I would be very grateful if all members would give this bill their urgent and, I hope, their favourable consideration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING CERTAIN IMMIGRATION LAWS AND PROCEDURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our party I want to make it clear from the outset that we are going to make every attempt to co-operate with the minister and the government in helping him and them out of the predicament in which they now find themselves.
I think it would be irresponsible on our part to put up a strong opposition to this remedial type of legislation to get the government out of a jam resulting from a court decision. Nevertheless, I think it would be less than responsible of the opposition if we did not take this opportunity to comment on the general procedures by which immigration law has been made and administered in this country, going back to the original source of legislation in this field, as far back as 1952.
To put the point very briefly, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the mess that the government now finds itself in as a result of two court decision which were made according to law, and which in my judgment are reasonable decisions, is a product of the fact that regulations have been made under this act, first enacted in 1952, which in many respects were never anticipated by that act.
This is one of the classic situations where the government has made laws by regulation. I think it is cited by lawyers throughout the dominion as the prime example of some of the dangers of law making by regulation, away from the scrutiny of Parliament, away from the public, done for supposed reasons of expedience, speed and flexibility, but with many inherent dangers which I will outline to the House later.
Indeed, I suggest that the bill we have before us is in many respect an admission by the government that the structure of regulations that it has built up since 1952, not in any orderly fashion but on the basis of mere ad hocery, may well be on the verge of collapse. I wonder, particularly in the next few months when this House is not sitting, what other judgments the Immigration Appeal Board and the Federal Court of Canada will hand down which hold that certain regulations are ultra vires the legislation which supposedly gave authority for them to be made.
It might be appropriate at this time to go back to some first principles in law making, which from time to time seem to have been forgotten by the government in the administration of the act. I take as my point of departure a study that is well known in the field of administrative law. Formally it is known as "A Report of the Committee on Ministers' Powers," made in 1932 in the United King-
5812

July 19, 1973
Immigration
dom and commonly referred to as the Donoughmore committee. It is a very relevant subject matter which I know a committee of a previous parliament had occasion to deal with when considering the whole subject matter of statutory instruments, a committee chaired by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) and which reported two or three years ago.
To refresh the memories of some hon. members on what the Donoughmore committee said, I am going to quote briefly from the section called "Summary of Arguments of the Critics of Delegated Legislation", or law-making by regulation. That committee at page 53 of the report suggested that:
Acts of Parliament may be passed only in skeleton form-
As the 1952 act was.
-and contain only the barest general principles. Other matters of principle, transcending procedure and the details of administration, matters which closely affect the rights and property of the subject, may be left to be worked out in the departments, with the result that laws are promulgated which have not been made by, and get little supervision from parliament. Some of the critics suggest that this practice has so far passed all reasonable limits, as to have assumed the character of a serious invasion of the sphere of Parliament by the executive. The extent of its adoption is, they argue, excessive, and leads not only to widespread suspicion and distrust of the machinery of government, but actually endangers our civic and personal liberties.
I believe those words were relevant in 1932 and they may well contain lessons for those of us wrestling with the problems before us in 1973.
I refer to another comment of the Donoughmore committee. The committee suggested that delegated power may be so loosely defined that the area it is intended to cover cannot be clearly known and uncertainty of this kind is unfair to those affected.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that is a relevant commentary on the immigration laws and form of regulations that we have had in this country. As proof of the pudding let me refer to the rather landmark regulations that were introduced by a former minister of manpower and immigration in 1967 and outline to the House the broad and expansive scope of those regulations which, in my opinion, should have been introduced in the form of legislation- legislation which was consistent and which contained clearly defined and enunciated principles for members of the committee and members of the House to follow.
I am going to refer to a release from the office of Manpower and Immigration in 1967 which purported to explain those regulations to members of the House and members of the public. But before I get into the particular problem of what the minister thought he was doing by introducing those regulations, I should add that Parliament passed companion legislation called the Immigration Appeal Board Act. That was the first Immigration Appeal Board, set up in 1967, which in my view negatived any argument that it was impossible to monitor the conduct of Parliament even to introduce such regulations.
First, in 1967 the minister purported to suggest that by regulation-not by law but by regulation-he would set up an assessment system to permit immigration officers to apply the same standards to potential immigrants from all

areas of the world. A pretty significant statement and a pretty significant enactment, but done by way of regulation!
Second, the 1967 regulations formula confirmed that Canadian citizens or permanent residents of Canada were entitled to bring their dependants to Canada. Again, an important matter of principle contained in regulations.
Third, in 1967 the regulations established that the privilege given citizens or permanent residents to apply for other more distant relatives to come to Canada was to be extended to all areas of the world, and new classes of relatives were to become eligible for this assistance. Again, an all-embracing matter of principle incorporated into law without the benefit of parliamentary scrutiny.
Finally, there was the linking of the selection standards to conditions within Canada to ensure that a flow of immigrants was made possible and was more closely related to the economic requirements of Canada. Very sweeping and significant measures, Mr. Speaker, not adopted by law but by regulation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we find the government today, in 1973, the victim of its own law-making processes which have been perpetuated now for 24 years. I think it is high time we had a change in thinking as to the way in which our immigration law is to be made. I am not too sanguine that we are going to have a change in thinking, however.
I was impressed by a comment made by the former minister of manpower and immigration, now the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), when he was speaking in this House on Bill C-197 and commenting on his experience as a former minister. If I may quote him to hon. members, on June 22, 1973, as reported at page 5034 of Hansard, the hon. member said:
I want to speak really of my own experience in a non-partisan way, provided the opposition will let me do that.
Well, we will let him, Mr. Speaker.
I hope what I say will be considered constructive criticism relating to a very important department of government. When I assumed the role of minister of immigration I also assumed an archaic, outmoded law which had been adopted in the year 1952. It was hardly a set of rules that was suitable to meet the challenge of a contemporary society.
What an admission, Mr. Speaker.
So, consequently, as some of the lawyers in this House know .. . many of the practices of the past three years have been based on regulations rather than on any concrete, specific provision within the law of 1952.
And then here is the great statement of prophecy of the hon. member for Verdun. I am sorry he is not here tonight. He said:
Regulations do have a tendency to run well beyond the intent of the law.
It is almost as if he had read the judgment of the Immigration Appeal Board that night and was sorry for what had happened. But what a statement of prophecy, Mr. Speaker. I was also impressed-and I say this as a credit to the present minister-when in committee he indicated that perhaps we may have some change in direction in law making on the part of the government in this field. He did say he was not going to make the usual sort of statement that about eight ministers had made before
July 19, 1973

him, that we were going to have a complete review of immigration policy and perhaps new regulations. He said he was going to have a green paper, and then continued: Therefore, it is my intention to have produced a public document that will raise a number of essential issues which have to be determined in the establishment of a long term immigration policy. This document will be designed to encourage a response from all sectors of the community who have an interest in such a vital subject. When we receive this variety of views, we will be in a position to recommend to Parliament legislation that should provide a basis for an immigration policy to meet Canada's future needs.
Mr. Speaker, I say hallelujah-a commitment from the minister to have legislation. I want to assure him that I and members of this House will hold him to his word. But it must not be skeleton legislation. It must consider the principles, rights, privileges and obligations of the people of Canada in their broadest and most public form possible under our law. As I say, Mr. Speaker, we will hold the minister to his word.
In committee, pursuing the discussion of Bill C-197, an act to amend the Immigration Appeal Board Act, there was another interesting exchange which I think should be brought to the attention of the House. This is the question, I think treated rather facetiously by the minister at the time, which was put by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). He questioned a particular subsection in the Immigration Appeal Board Act in which the governor-in-Council was given power by regulation to amend or vary any regulations made under the Immigration Act. The hon. member for Hamilton West, quite rightly in my view, questioned whether it was proper in the legal sense in one act to be granting authority to amend or vary regulations in another act. The minister and his deputy, who was present at the time of course, replied that they had had legal opinions that it was quite proper to include that particular clause in the legislation. I cannot help but quote the minister's statement at that time. He said:
May I just say, Mr. Alexander, that I hope and pray you will never be in a postion to say, "I told you so"-as a slight aside to my legal advisers.
The hon. member for Hamilton West is not here, so I am going to take this opportunity to say on his behalf, "I told you so".
There is one last matter which I think is important. It deals with another important act which was a product of the last Parliament. I refer to the Statutory Instruments Act. That was a product of a recommendation by a committee which was ably chaired by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan). That act created a number of obligations on the executive to ensure that proposed regulations were properly perused, scrutinized, publicized and reviewed, with the object of ascertaining their legality before becoming law and affecting the rights of people.
In particular, I want to make references to section 3 of the Staturory Instruments Act. I might say that was law at the beginning of November when the purported repeal of section 34 of the regulations and the amendment to section 28(1) of the regulations took place. Section 3 requires, and I quote:
Immigra tion
Where a regulation-making authority proposes to make a regulation it shall cause to be forwarded to the Clerk of the Privy Council three copies of the proposed regulation in both official languages. . ..
-the Clerk of the Privy Council, in consultation with the Deputy Minister of Justice, shall examine the proposed regulation to ensure that
(a) it is authorized by the statute pursuant to which it is to be
made;
I ask the minister to indicate in committee whether this was in fact done. Was there in fact a proper examination by the Clerk of the Privy Council, in consultation with the Deputy Minister of Justice, to see whether the amendment to regulation 28(1) was authorized by section 57 of the Immigration Act? Or was it the case, as it states in subsection (b), that:
-it does not constitute an unusual or unexpected use of the authority pursuant to which it is to be made;
To my knowledge, we have not tested the provisions of the Statutory Instruments Act. This may be a good opportunity to begin.
I would be very interested, as would other hon. members, in hearing the minister's comments as to the extent to which the Statutory Instruments Act was complied with. To my mind, it raises some suspicion as to whether the whole process of decision making by regulation in the government really complies in substance and in fact with the Statutory Instruments Act.
This matter will, of course, be the task of the statutory instruments committee, which is a standing committee of this House and the Senate. As a member of that committee, I look forward to participating in the scrutiny of that which Parliament designates it to do. This is an opportunity we ought not let pass on the bill before us.
In conclusion, I may say it was a make-shift manner in which the government introduced the November regulations. It was done hurriedly, rather like a guillotine. Possibly the government did not have much time to give any thought to the regulations prior to October 30. They were engaged in other things. As I said at the outset, what we have here is a classic example of the danger of law making by regulation. I think this will become a very valuable lesson for future governments and future Parliaments.
Our party will co-operate with the government in seeing that this bill is quickly passed through all three stages in order that we can, as the minister suggested, achieve the objectives that the recent amendments to the Immigration Appeal Board Act sought to achieve.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to take a very few moments to outline the position of this party with regard to this bill.
The reason for Bill C-212 is two decisions, one of the Immigration Appeal Board and the other of the Federal Court of Canada, both of which made a very strict legal interpretation of the act and regulations. I recall that when we set up the Immigration Appeal Board in 1967, it was to be a court of record rather than an administrative body. There was some debate at that time about whether we should make it that. Since the time it was set up it has developed a body of law. I might say it has helped lawyers who prepare and present cases before the Immigration
26454-4 i

July 19, 1973
Immigra tion
Appeal Board. However, it seems the Immigration Appeal Board is serving as a half-way house between an administrative body and a court of record.
I do not intend to cast any reflection of the Immigration Appeal Board because the composition of that board and its work has been excellent. They have developed a good body of law. They have made it very easy for appellants to appear before them and present their case in a strictly non-legal way. That was probably our intention when we set up the Immigration Appeal Board. Sometimes in a court of law it happens that lawyers argue with regard to the admissibility of evidence and some of the strict legal points. Clients just cannot appreciate or understand the complexities of law and evidence. The Immigration Appeal Board attempted to overcome that when appellants appeared before them. As a result they have developed a very strong body of law and at the same time have tried to retain an administrative approach with regard to the tendering of evidence and so forth.
In both decisions the Immigration Appeal Board took a very strict legal interpretation. The result is that there could be chaos with regard to the cases before them. The minister indicated that if we were to follow the decisions of the Immigration Appeal Board and the Federal Court, nearly 12,000 cases would be in jeopardy, and this would destroy the good intent of Bill C-197 which was basically to clear up the immigration mess.
One of the fine features of the present government is that, every time they have a problem, five or six previous ministers have been involved and the problem has compounded over the years. With regard to immigration, we have had a tremendous mess. No person can really point a finger at one or more of the immigration ministers, especially the present minister and the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey). It has been very awkward to pin down the responsibility for the problems that has developed over the past four or five years.
If any person has any appreciation of immigration problems, he will appreciate what has happened to our immigration laws over the past three or four years. Prior to October 30, places in Canada such as Montreal were being flooded by persons who came here for the obstensible purpose of being visitors, but really to get landed immigrant status. There was a tremendous flow of people, and this compounded the difficulty. On November 3, immediately after the election, regulation 34 was changed, with a related change to regulation 28. I think that had the N.D.P. or the Conservative party been in power at that time, they would have done the same thing. There was nothing else which could be done. With all these people in Canada, the government was obliged to take a realistic approach, and I think the contents of Bill C-197 embodies such an approach.
We now have a law which would give would-be immigrants presently in Canada the right to adjust their status. Most of them will probably remain here, and that is a good thing. The minister is before us tonight because of two difficult decisions, decisions which were probably correct in the strict sense of the law, but very difficult to apply in the field of administration. I hope that the Federal Courts
(Mr. Gilbert.]
of Appeal and the Immigration Appeal Board do not regard this as a slap in the face reflecting on their own approach to the law. I hope they see that, if we were to follow those two judgments, the beneficial effects of Bill C-197 would be lost and we would find ourselves in a worse position than we were on November 3, 1972.
We in this party wish to co-operate so that we can get rid of the problem which exists at the moment, apply Bill C-197 to its full effect, and then get on to the next step. I wish I had understood the erudite exposition of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) concerning the regulations and so forth. This is why we have professors in the House, men who are strong on theory. We also have men who are experienced in practice. The member for St. Paul's presented an erudite exposition of the theoretical aspect of the regulations, and I hope the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) will take up the challenge presented to the House, study the measure in depth and assist in coming forward with a solution.
More important, there is need for a long term program. The Minister has undertaken to study this question. He says he will make no rash promises as to the date upon which a new law may come forward, but he will look into the matter and see that something emerges by way of a study in depth. Once this has been undertaken it is up to us as members to relate our experience and thinking to it and bring forth an Immigration Act which will be applicable in 1974-75.
I think all Canadians want an act of which they can be proud, because immigration is really the keystone of a growing Canada. If we have a satisfactory act, one which can attract the right people, we shall continue to grow in prosperity and culture and this land will be better as a result. We in this party support the bill for those reasons.

Mr. Speaker, we do not intend to delay the passage of Bill C-212 because we believe it is very urgent to pass it in order to settle many cases of immigration in Canada. Increasing the number of members of the Immigration Appeal Board will be of great help, in my opinion, in solving, current immigration problems as soon as possible, and will also help prevent those which could occur in future and maybe as early as this fall.
Mr. Speaker, we will therefore give our complete support to the minister presenting Bill C-212, and we wish that this new act on the Immigration Appeal Board will contribute greatly to the introduction in Canada of select people, of people liable to become good Canadians. We need people who want to take part in the development of Canada. We want to have a larger population than we now have. Certain immigrants are desirable and I believe that, with an improved board, and one which will take care of them, these people will become good Canadian citizens and will contribute to the economic and social development of our country, which will be, I believe, to the benefit of all Canadians.

Well, they will be able to bring the bill on for consideration some time tomorrow.
The minister will expect to be chastised. He has been chastised only mildly so far. Not because of what he himself has done. It is unfortunate for the minister that he is the last of a long line of ministers who have really done some terrible things affecting the immigration practices of this country. I do not know how many ministers we have had. If we look over the last 10 or 15 years we find that the department of immigration has been a stepchild. This has resulted in a tragic situation, one from which we are now suffering. The present minister is, I think, trying to do a good job. I do not blame the civil servants; they have lacked ministers who could give them effective direction. Of course, I am not criticizing the minister personally. He must be given credit for coming forward promptly and saying mea culpa, admitting he was wrong and asking for a remedy.
In his speech tonight the minister said words to the effect, "A couple of decisions are giving us trouble." I sympathize with his position. When I practised law I disagreed with every decision which went against me.
