I may disagree with those decisions too, but am not allowed to say so. The minister also said something like, "We are not going to repeat the experience." I do not know whether the "we" refers to the ministerial "we" or the parliamentary "we". As it is not a parliamentary experience to which the minister is referring, surely he is speaking of a government experience. That must be made plain.
As to disagreeing with decisions that give us trouble, let us recognize that the rule of law and of Parliament is supreme. That fact is often forgotten. Let me recount something that happened a short time ago. This story may be irrelevant, but it bears on the attitude of this govern-
Immigration
ment. In Yellowknife a judge who is a good friend of mine, Mr. Justice Morrow, was engaged in a case, an issue with which, under the law, he had a right to deal. He was properly seized of jurisdiction. The government, fearing what he was likely to do, or fearing his decision, went before a judge of the Federal Court and asked for an order of prohibition which would prevent Mr. Justice Morrow from hearing the case.
That was not right. Merely because you do not like a judgment or what a judge will do or has done is no reason for saying, "This is bad; this is hurting what the government has done." I do not believe in that, and I do not think other members of the House do. The minister does not take that attitude as an individual, but that has become part of this government's thinking. Of course, in the not too distant future when we form the government, we may adopt the same attitude. However, I do not think so and hope not.
I remember when the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), who was then a private member, sat on a committee of this House and of the other place, established in the fall of 1966 and commencing its deliberations in November, 1966, on the issue of immigration. That was a good committee. It heard many witnesses. It did not have the great urge to travel, as is the case with many committees now, but it nevertheless went to Toronto and Montreal and heard briefs from many groups representing ethnic organizations and other organizations in the country. It called the minister responsible at that time, who is the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), and the deputy minister, who has gone on to greater things under the aegis of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen).
I had not been in the House for too long then and was still fairly innocent. I thought the committee would do something. The government had said, "The Immigration Act passed in 1952 is giving us great trouble. We want to examine important areas of concern to do with how the state should exercise its prerogative in selecting people, what manner of people should come into this country, and under what circumstances." We sat from November until May, 1967. As I said, the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was a good member of that committee, not having suffered as a result of becoming a minister; he was then a private member. Probably when he comes over to my side of the House, he will once again become a good member.
The committee did not make too many recommendations, having been advised against it. We discussed lots of issues. I well remember the first appearance of the present Minister of Transport before that committee. He said, as recorded on page 9 of the evidence taken on November 15, 1966:
The deliberations of this Committee will, I hope, lead both to Parliamentary action, revising the basic legislation needed in immigration and also to administrative arrangements and procedures that will receive the widest possible support from the Canadian people.
Both the minister and the deputy minister wanted to distract attention from the fact, as became evident shortly after, that they were engaged in processing the passage of the Immigration Appeal Board Act which has created the

July 19, 1973
Immigration
difficulties in which the government now finds itself. That committee was a subterfuge.
Among the witnesses called was the present leader of the Conservative party in Manitoba, Mr. Spivak. I am not talking in any partisan sense when I say that when he appeared he made a tremendous impression on the civil servants and members of the committee. He made a good presentation and pointed out something which many of us had forgotten, namely, that immigration can and ought to be an effective economic weapon. Properly used, it can do effectively what this government has been trying to do without success for many years-deal with economic disparities in the country. He pointed that out and buttressed his presentation with evidence and facts. Members of the committee of all parties and the members from the other place as well were all impressed with what Mr. Spivak had to say.
I recall, in questioning Mr. Spivak, that a sensible suggestion was made. I am referring to the fact that, under the British North America Act, jurisdiction, over immigration is divided between provincial legislatures and the federal Parliament. I do not know if anyone has ever determined where the supremacy in this field lies. Certainly, the federal government has invaded the field and occupied it. Nevertheless, provincial legislatures are interested in the question of immigration.
I suggested that there ought to be a standing council, made up of federal and provincial ministers or civil servants and that they should look at questions of immigration. I do not know whether anything was done about that. I doubt it. I expect that recommendation was treated in the way all recommendations by that committee were treated.
On the last day of the hearings the present Minister of Transport appeared before the committee and told us what a tremendous job we had done, how thankful he was for our contribution, and how much would come out of it. He said, "Don't worry, you will be reconstituted next year and we will pay attention to your recommendations."
Apparently all this work was to lead to a new Immigration Act. This happened in 1967, 15 years after the last bill in this area had been passed. It is in existence today. The minister said, "Yes, we are going to accept your recommendations; we want new legislation." So the committee brought in its third report, which said in part:
Your Committee therefore recommends that it be reconstituted next session and the evidence adduced during the present session, in both French and English, be referred to it, so that it will be in a position to pursue its work on this important matter, namely Canadian Immigration Policy.
That report was submitted by the chairman of the committee on May 8, 1967. We came back the next session and that committee was never reconstituted. Its recommendations withered on the vine. All the thousands of words of evidence that had been taken were simply scrapped and forgotten.
That is the trouble with this government and with the immigration department in particular. I have a great deal of respect for the officials of the immigration department. I have respect for the ministers, with some reservations.

However, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to questions dealing with immigration it lies with this Parliament, with its knowledge, experience and capacity, to interpret the views of the public with which they deal, to best suit the interests of this country in dealing with immigration policy. I think it has been a tragic mistake.
I suggest this is one of the reasons we have this difficulty today. What has been the result? The recommendations of the committee, as I have mentioned, were entirely forgotten. The Immigration Appeal Board was set up. It did a good job at first and then slowly, by order in council, by regulation and by decree, the widest possible licence was granted in respect of people seeking the right to come into this country or ultimately being in this country to be able to secure the right to ask to remain here. If they were then rejected, through procedures established by the act, they placed themselves on the assembly line of the procedure of appeal available through the Immigration Appeal Board Act.
As a result this backlog of thousands and thousands of cases was built up. Several situations ensued. There was a situation last year in which I was involved. I asked questions a number of times. I remember one particular occasion within the last 12 or 14 months when there was evidence that a man had not only been allowed to come into this country but in fact had been surreptitiously smuggled in by the government under an assumed name. This man was called Pershing Gervais, whose mottled history both socially and in criminal terms left an awful lot to be desired. Because of arrangements made between officials of this government and officials of the United States government this man, who had been an investigator on the staff of the district attorney of New Orleans and was involved in an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the assassination of the president of the united States, for reasons no one has ever been able to tell us in this House, was smuggled in and provided with a job with the Canadian counterpart of a United States firm. This man lived in Vancouver, thousands of miles from his job. He received a salary of $18,000 a year. His family was smuggled in under an assumed name. He was given landed immigrant status through illegal use of the Immigration Act and regulations. That was one case.
What do we find on the other page? We find a case of an unfortunate young Polish woman who had entered Canada properly as a visitor. Her application for appeal and leave to stay in this country had been objected to. She was so concerned, discouraged and disappointed about what she thought was her fate if she returned to Poland that she committed suicide.
There are two opposite sides to problems that have arisen under the Immigration Act in its present form, in addition to the thousands of cases which are the subject of discussion tonight. I have spoken to the minister about this and I think he genuinely believes that something must be done. While there must be left in the hands of the administration some opportunity to act with flexibility and speed, nevertheless it is essential that it be left to this House to deal with new legislation, and in that new legislation take into account the facts which we have experienced and which have been dealt with by the minis-

ter and other members tonight, facts of which hon. members of this House are aware.

ENERGY-PROPOSED MACKENZIE VALLEY OIL PIPE LINE-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF INFORMATION RELATING TO UNITED STATES INQUIRIES AS TO GOVERNMENT'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address the House for a few minutes tonight on a matter about which we have heard a great deal in the last several days, namely the appalling situation in connection with any hope Canada might have of stopping the Alaska TAPS proposal from resulting in tankers going down the coast of British Columbia and the west coast of Canada.
In 1971 this House instructed the government to send a formal note of protest to the United States government in Washington since we took the position that we were opposed to a tanker route down the west coast of British Columbia. Since that day, I want to remind hon. members that ministers of the government have repeatedly assured us that they are doing everything possible to have this tanker route stopped.
We all know what the situation has been in the last few days. We all know that the Senate has passed a bill overriding environmental considerations and everything else in order to push the tanker route proposal through. One of the most vigorous members of the Liberal party in opposition to the tanker route was the former member for Esquimalt-Saanich, Mr. David Anderson, who is now the leader of the Liberal party in British Columbia. All hon. members know that he staged for a considerable time a proper, decent and vigorous fight, which he continued since he left federal politics, against this tanker route.
In apparent admiration for the work that he was doing in the province of B.C. the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) replied to a qeustion that I put to him on March 2, 1973, as reported at page 1835 of Hansard, when I was asking what was happening with the tanker route proposal. After telling me that he was interested in my belated interest in the tanker route-which seems rather amusing in view of the fact that I come from the west coast where people do not have a belated interest in the tanker route but a very real interest-he said:
Of course, the hon. member is aware of the fact that the Liberal leader in British Columbia is responsible for the very good turn of events in this matter.
I do not know what good turn of events the right hon. Prime Minister was referring to in that answer, but I can tell hon. members today that there are no happy events. I want to remind them that according to the July 16, 1973 edition of the Vancouver Sun, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), in referring to the proposal of the leader of the Liberal party in British Columbia to try to use the Mackenzie route as a last ditch stand to avoid the tanker route, told delegates:
.. . that what Anderson suggested was a bluff . . .
Here we have the provincial Liberal leader doing his best in the province of British Columbia, and at the same time the federal minister telling people in B.C. that all he is doing is bluffing. Now we have the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), who entered this debate in recent months, referred to in the same edition of the Vancouver Sun in the following terms:

July 19, 1973
Adjournment Debate
In the audience was Environment Minister Davis, who has publicly suggested using the gas line to apply pressure.
On March 29, Davis told the Vancouver Kiwanis Club that the gas line is Canada's "trump card" in the battle to keep tankers out of west coast inland waters.
Here we have at the western conference of Liberals in my city a complete and utter confrontation with respect to policy.
All hon. members will remember the incredible episode of a few months ago when the Prime Minister told us that a committee had been set up to study tanker route controls. He could not find that committee and he could not find out what had happened to it, but finally the Minister of the Environment told us on March 8, as reported in Hansard at page 2017, when we were talking about this committee:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The word "committee" is inappropriate.
It was "inappropriate" because the committee did not even exist. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said today that continual representations have been made since the summer of 1972. The Prime Minister said on television yesterday that these have been continued. Yet not so long ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was asked about this, and this is what he said, as reported in Hansard of February 14 at page 1281:
The government has no intention of renewing its representations.
That is to the United States. He went on to say:
Of course, we will be interested in hearing from the United States administration in this regard, but at present we do not plan to take any fresh initiative.
All I can say is that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was misleading the House or else was unbelievably unaware of what was going on to an extent that is almost inconceivable.
There has been talk of a railroad. You remember that questions were asked on May 22 of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). The minister replied:
-my response to the right hon. gentleman is yes, there is such an evaluation under way.
He continued:
In collaboration with my colleague, the Minister of Transport, that proposal is being evaluated.
Yet today we have an incredible release put out by those four horsemen of disaster, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), who have apparently been sent forth by a blind commander, the Prime Minister. This release says in part:
A study will begin immediately on the engineering feasibility and the cost of a railroad to move oil and natural gas southward from the Arctic over the perma frost region.
In view of these incredibly conflicting statements by the government over the last four or five months, I ask where is the credibility, where is the competence, where is the sincerity? I demand, on behalf of everybody living on the west coast-even if this does not matter to a government which is so concerned with central Canada-the tabling of all documents exchanged between the government and the

United States government; and I demand the personal intervention of the Prime Minister, even at this eleventh hour, to do something about this disastrous situation.

In terms of the original question which the hon. member raised concerning the time at which the last correspondence or communication between the United States government and this government took place, he is aware, of course, that that material was provided on June 22, and again on June 27. The original replies were transmitted to the United States embassy in Ottawa on June 27, and the revised version was transmitted by the Canadian embassy in Washington to the United States state department on July 6.
As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated to this House earlier today, the answers given to the Unites States government were almost entirely repetitions of answers given to Parliament and to U.S. officials. I would also inform the hon. member that the House of Commons is monitored by U.S. officials, just as we monitor the U.S. Congress, and they are fully aware of our position.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker on Tuesday, July 10, as recorded in Hansard at page 5453, I put this question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
Mr. Speaker, I have a question that is supplementary to those that have been asked with reference to the rising cost of living and I address it to the Prime Minister because it relates to a matter which comes under the administrative responsibility of at least six different cabinet ministers. In view of the fact that a 2 per cent ceiling on the annual escalation of any pension is out of date, and in view of the rapidity with which the cost of living is rising, will the Prime Minister arrange for the government to consider as a matter of high priority the removing of that 2 per cent ceiling from the annual escalation of all pensions to which it still applies?
July 19, 1973

Hansard records the answer to that question as follows:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REMOVAL OF 2 PER CENT CEILING ON ANNUAL ESCALATION OF PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the government took the very worth-while and bold action of tying down many pensions to the increase in the cost of living, I am sure the hon. member will realize that we are considering this total matter. However, the matter of availability of funds to deal with all categories of people at the same time is the one which the government must also keep in mind.
I offered a retort to that in which I expressed the hope that the Prime Minister might be here for a discussion of this matter some night at the time of adjournment. I realize now that I am going to have to settle for the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Reid), but maybe it is not all that bad. Maybe I will get a better answer from him than I got from the Prime Minister.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary to argue the basic point which I set out in my question, namely that with the cost of living rising 5 per cent, 6 per cent or 7 per cent a year it is no longer sensible or just for pension escalations to be limited to 2 per cent per year. So long as this situation obtains it simply means that pensioners under these conditions are falling behind year after year.
It is true, as the Prime Minister said the other day, that i* was a Liberal government that first brought in the escalation of some pensions; but when the Prime Minister boasts of that I ask that he also take the blame for the fact that they put a 2 per cent ceiling on the amount by which such pensions could escalate.
Now the fact is, and I welcome it, that we have got rid of that 2 per cent ceiling with respect to four pensions that I can indicate, namely, old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, the war veterans' allowance and war disability pensions that are paid under the Pension Act. That is fine. Those pensions now escalate in accordance with the actual rise in the cost of living. I put in parenthesis, as I always do when I speak on this subject, that I am not satisfied even with an increase which measures up to the cost of living. I think the escalation of pensions should equal the rise in the standard of living; but at least let us get to the point where pensions escalate to the full extent of the rise in the cost of living.
In my question to the Prime Minister I said I was putting it to him because it related to a matter that comes under the administrative responsibility of at least six different cabinet ministers. May I indicate those? The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is responsible for the Canada pension plan and escalations under that legislation are still limited to 2 per cent. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) is responsible for the pension increases that are paid retired public servants and a number of other related groups and those increases are limited to 2 per cent per year. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) is responsible for pensions paid to retired armed forces personnel. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) is responsible for pensions paid to retired RCMP personnel. Again, in those two categories the 2 per cent limit applies on the annual escalation. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), in my view, is responsible for Canadian National Railways pensions, and those are limited to an escalation of 2 per
Adjournment Debate
cent per year. Even that 2 per cent is on an ad hoc basis; it has not been made permanent.
I could have mentioned Devco, which comes under the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), and the retired employees of the Bank of Canada, who come under the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). Certain retired diplomats come under the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), so my list of six is growing to eight or nine. In case, any pensioners are missed, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) is responsible for a regulation that says that no pension plan can qualify for income tax purposes unless it limits its escalation to 2 per cent per year.
Yet the Prime Minister has the gall to stand up here the other day and boast about what the government has done in making a start in tying some pensions to the cost of living, when along with that step the same government has imposed this miserable 2 per cent ceiling which, as I say, is affecting pensioners on all kinds of pensions, both public and private.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council has that better answer that I anticipated. I suggest this is an area where action must be taken and taken soon, namely the removal of the 2 per cent ceiling from the annual escalation of all pensions, both public and private.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to suggest to the House I have been around here as long as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but I was around when the 2 per cent annual increment for pensions was introduced into the House of Commons. I recall what a revolutionary theory that was and what an impact it had on the development of pension plans in Canada.
Just as a long journey starts with a first step, we took that first step in removing the 2 per cent limitation on the pensions which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has indicated; that is, on pensions paid to senior citizens, the guaranteed income supplement, the war veterans pension and the was veterans disability allowance.
I hope that in short order we will be able to come to an accommodation with the provinces and have the 2 per cent limitation removed from the Canada pension plan. That will probably be the big difficulty. It is currently under negotiation. If those negotiations are successful with the provinces, I hope legislation will be brought in some time this session, probably in the fall.
With regard to pensions of defence employees, RCMP and other government people, I remind the hon. member he was helpful in sending to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates a resolution dealing with those pensions, although not particularly on the point he mentioned. I assure the hon. member the government is cognizant of the problem. It is sympathetic toward getting a proper solution to that problem. I hope that in this Parliament we will come to a solution that will not only satisfy the hon.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mb'. Stan Schellenberger (Wetaskiwin): Mr. Speaker, on Friday, June 22, as recorded at page 5022 of Hansard, I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the fact that capitalization costs for young farmers have increased by 66 per cent in the past ten years and young farmers cannot always get Farm Credit Corporation loans or afford 10 per cent plus interest rates, will the minister be announcing a program soon to help young farmers stay on the farm or get starting in farming?
The minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the record shows that more young farmers have received farm credit loans this year than for many years. We are working on a program. We will be meeting with our provincial counterparts to discuss this program on how we can aid more young people who really want to enter farming or remain in farming to do that.
In my short period of years, I have heard politicians say over and over again that they are working on programs to get young farmers started in farming. For years they have stood on platforms and said that, although we have been successful in the past, we are working on a new program to stop the mass exodus of young people leaving the farms and going to the cities.
Perhaps it is necessary to have a definition of a family farm. One person has described the family farm as a way of life, an independent business in the conduct of which a farmer has a chance to live a decent life with a reasonable income, financially dependent less upon the vagaries of the market than on his own efforts to produce.
Canadians should never forget that the family farm, as opposed to the corporate farm, still produces the bulk of Canada's agricultural output. It is ironic that many economists still point to the agricultural sector as one of the last examples of effective private enterprise with substantial economic competition.
Unless something basic is done, this characteristic of the sector will disappear just as surely as it has disappeared in other productive sectors. The continuing decrease in the number of farms in Alberta has gone almost unnoticed in the past few years. Figures show that in 1972 there were 67,702 farms in Alberta compared with 84,000 in 1951. This means we have suffered a decrease amounting to nearly
1,000	farms per year.
The chief factor in this decline has been the ever-increasing amount of capital necessary to begin farming. In 1951, the capital figure was $21,000. In 1961 it was $37,000 and today it is estimated that one needs $80,000. Since an initial outlay of this magnitude is needed, many people, especially young people, who would like to begin farming are unable to do so.
As we all know, the main lending institution is the Farm Credit Corporation. It is to the credit of past governments and of the present government that the number of loans has tripled over the last decade or so. However, I come

from an area which is populated by many family farmers and I have received numerous complaints from young farmers, or would-be farmers, that credit is very difficult to obtain. This personal but very real testimony to the inadequacy of government programs should sharpen our critical faculties in the present discussion.
A glance at some statistics indicates that in 1972-73 at least 60 per cent of the loans went to persons who were over 35 years of age. The average age of Canadian farmers is 49, and this figure, rather than decreasing, is increasing. Every social scientist has documented the exodus of young people from the farms to the cities. It has been said that every day 42 farmers leave their occupations.
Not only are farms being bought out and older established farmers increasing the size of their farms, but, more significantly, the programs implemented by the government have reinforced and perhaps encouraged this trend instead of counteracting it. But before we go any further, let us listen to the words of an individual who is actually engaged in the farm credit business. Mr. G. W. Arnold, manager of the agricultural department on the Royal Bank of Canada, told the international credit congress last May that government-backed loans were of decreasing importance because the nature of the farm unit is radically changing. The farmer, he said, was a businessman with a large capital investment in land.
My bank manager says he is leery of lending under the farm improvement and farm credit legislation because of the restriction on the interest rate to one per cent above the prime rate. It is clear that if young people are to be encouraged to enter farming it will be necessary to provide sufficient capital at prime rates or below for those in the lower age groups. Perhaps we could subsidize interest rates for these young people, who would pay the loan back later from their substantially greater yields. This is not a new idea. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) moved an amendment to Bill C-5 on June 26, 1972, to the effect that where a borrower under the age of 30 years first obtains a loan under this act, the governor-incouncil shall not prescribe a rate of interest in respect of that loan in excess of 5 per cent.
If the F.C.C. is in theory an adequate means by which to supply those who are willing to farm with the credit to do so, then in practice it fails to do so. The practical proof of what I have said lies in the fact that many young farmers are increasingly turning to small farm loans agencies which some provinces, such as Alberta, are setting up to handle the making of loans to people whose applications have been rejected by the F.C.C. and other agencies.
If we really want to do something effective to counteract the trend toward the dissolution of the small farm, we must institute effective incentives. Prices have increased, but costs have kept pace. With the recent escalation in food and feed shortages, costs to farmers have increased even more markedly. Many of these farmers do not have the collateral base to obtain loans. Perhaps we might consider the actual land, equipment and livestock as collateral and not require a large, previously built-up capital base. I feel the government should adopt the following-

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR PROGRAM TO ASSIST YOUNG PEOPLE WISHING TO BE FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the remarks made by the hon. member, because this is an opportunity to explain to hon. members some of the very important things this government has undertaken in order to help young farmers become established in farming.
One of the first things I did on being appointed Minister of Agriculture was to look into the Farm Credit Corporation, and all offices in Canada were to be visited. I think all western offices so far have been covered. We wanted to find out how many requests were coming in from young farmers. I asked farm organizations and provincial governments to make suggestions to me on how we might amend this legislation, or even bring in brand new legislation, so as to make it attractive for young farmers to begin farming.
Amendments have been made to the Farm Credit Act which increased the loan ceiling of an individual's borrowings from $40,000 to $100,000. The Farm Credit Act was also changed to permit the minimum age at which a farmer is eligible for a loan to be consistent with provincial legislation governing the age at which persons may contract for mortgage loans. This amendment was made because several provinces have lowered the age of majority to below 21 years. This change now makes it possible for younger farmers to qualify for loans.
I should like to draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that in 1972-73 over 41 per cent of all Farm Credit Corporation loans were made to farmers under the age of
Adjournment Debate
35. The hon. member turned this fact around; he only used the bad figures. In 1970-71 less than 35 per cent of loans were to this age group. So the number of loans to younger farmers who wish to enter agriculture is on the upswing.
In the province of Alberta, the province from which the hon. member comes, there have been over 1,000 applications to date under the small farms program. These have mostly been made by young farmers.
The small farm development program offers another means whereby young farmers can acquire land or expand existing farming operations. This program seeks to assist farmers in acquiring land at reasonable prices and credit terms. I have also indicated that I and my officals will be meeting with our provincial counterparts in Charlottetown next week to discuss how better we can aid young people who want to enter or remain in farming.
May I also point out that recently the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) made it possible for a father to pass to his son or daughter who are engaged in farming the family farm without paying a tax, something that no other country in the world has done.
I emphasize, in closing, that we believe the best way to retain young people in agriculture is to make sure that farming is put on a paying basis. As farm income reach a level consistent with those earned by other sectors of society, there will be an incentive for younger people to take up farming. I, as Minister of Agriculture and as a politician, intend to do something about this, not just talk about it. I welcome this occasion for making these comments, Mr. Speaker.
